description: Earth Jukebox lets anyone hear our planet. Pick a region on the map, choose a phenomenon (wildfires, rainfall, temperature) and press play: real NASA Earth observation data becomes music, synchronized with a live animation on the map. Value sets pitch, intensity sets volume, event frequency sets rhythm. Then switch worlds: the same data is replayed with the sound character of the Moon, Mars or Jupiter, based on gravity. Data you can see, and now hear.
summary:
Earth Jukebox is an interactive web application developed by team CAT Beat that transforms NASA Earth Science visualizations into real-time, generative lo-fi music. Built using the Web Audio API without any pre-recorded audio files, the platform turns a virtual cozy studio into a scientific data sonification engine.

Users place different "vinyls"—representing NASA datasets like night lights, aerosols, and air quality—onto a virtual turntable. As a playback bar scans the world map from west to east, pixel brightness, color, and latitude are synthesized into musical notes, while atmospheric phenomena like lightning, carbon dioxide, and atmospheric rivers add percussive rhythms. An interactive Sandbox mode also lets users compose their own environmental tracks.

By translating complex satellite imagery into an engaging, accessible sensory experience, Earth Jukebox bridges the gap between Earth science and the general public, fostering emotional connection and awareness around global environmental changes.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

Earth Jukebox is an interactive web-based application that transforms NASA Earth science data visualizations into real-time, generative lo-fi music. Instead of playing pre-recorded audio files, the app turns a cozy virtual studio into a data sonification engine using the browser's Web Audio API.

  • The Vinyl Workflow: Users select a virtual vinyl record representing a NASA dataset (such as night lights, aerosols, or air quality) from a shelf. The vinyl moves to the turntable, the sleeve rests on a tripod, and the main screen updates from gray to the dataset's color map.
  • Sonification Engine: When the user hits Play, a scanning bar sweeps across the map from west to east. Each pixel's brightness, color, and latitude are translated in real-time into musical notes and parameters (e.g., higher pixel brightness increases volume/celesta intensity; latitude dictates pitch).
  • Percussion & Atmospheric Layers: Users can toggle environmental percussion tracks—such as lightning (SVS 5011), carbon dioxide heartbeats (SVS 5196), and atmospheric river rain (SVS 4960)—to build a complete lo-fi groove.
  • Sandbox Mode: Users can swap the turntable for a composition console featuring a 4-row grid (lights, aerosols, air quality, and percussion). Placed sounds map time horizontally and pitch vertically, letting anyone compose custom environmental tracks.
  • Interactive Environment: Features include a timeline scrubber for historical night lights (2012–2023), a window curtain that transitions the studio from night to day, and a telescope viewer for deep-space NASA/Hubble data (Caldwell 73).

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Accessibility & Engagement: Complex scientific data from satellites and numerical models can often feel intimidating or abstract. Earth Jukebox converts scientific metrics into an intuitive, relaxing sensory experience that anyone can enjoy.
  • Educational Immersion: By allowing users to interact directly with the data—scrubbing through years of night-light evolution or layering aerosols with flutes and wind effects—it creates an active learning loop rather than passive observation.
  • Lightweight & Cross-Platform: Running entirely in the browser via client-side code and Web Audio API synthesis means zero heavy audio asset downloads, ensuring fast load times and seamless cross-device compatibility.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The goal of Earth Jukebox is to bridge the gap between heavy Earth science research and the general public, fostering emotional resonance and environmental awareness. By turning datasets about climate change, air pollution, and urban sprawl into something warm, creative, and musical, the project aims to inspire curiosity about our planet's health, spark interest in NASA's open data repositories, and encourage community creativity around environmental stewardship.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming Languages:
    • HTML5 & CSS3 (for the structural layout, responsive styling, and fluid studio animations).
    • JavaScript (ES6+) (for image canvas analysis, state management, and algorithmic sound mapping).
    • Web Audio API (for real-time programmatic sound synthesis, oscillators, filters, and gain nodes).
    • HTML5 Canvas API (for scanning pixel data from NASA visual frames).
  • Hosting & Tools: Local server (python3 -m http.server) for development; Git/GitHub for version control and deployment.
  • Data Sources & Imagery: NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS), including frames for Night Lights (SVS 5313, SVS 5276), Aerosols (SVS 5669), Air Quality (SVS 5533), Lightning (SVS 5011), Carbon Dioxide (SVS 5196), Atmospheric Rivers (SVS 4960), and Hubble's Caldwell 73 (SVS 13786).

5. How is your project creative?

Earth Jukebox creatively subverts traditional data visualization tropes. Instead of presenting graphs or dashboards on a sterile interface, it reframes climate and Earth observation data as music. Blending the cozy, aesthetic vibes of lo-fi hip-hop culture with rigorous scientific datasets creates an unexpected and delightful juxtaposition. Furthermore, the Sandbox mode empowers users to become "data musicians," turning satellite imagery into personal artistic compositions.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Acoustic Harmony vs. Scientific Accuracy: Balancing data representation so that pollutants or dense clouds don't sound harsh or jarring, tuning the algorithmic mappings so the output remains consistently relaxing and "lo-fi."
  • User Experience & Storytelling: Designing an interactive narrative space (the virtual room, shelf, turntable, curtain, and telescope) rather than a boring menu system to make exploration feel organic and magical.
  • Technical Constraints: Handling browser audio policies and canvas security restrictions (requiring a local server or proper CORS handling) to ensure seamless real-time image pixel analysis without relying on bulky audio files.
